newsitem.title: USA: Republicans celebrate historic win in Congress.
newsitem.headline: Republicans celebrate historic win in Congress.

text.p: Elated Republicans celebrated a historic victory in Congress on Wednesday after increasing their majority in the Senate and fending off a Democratic challenge in the House of Representatives.

Continued Republican control promised to provide a sharp check on President Bill Clinton's plans for his second term, which he won in Tuesday's elections, and stepped-up investigations of ethical questions involving the White House.
It will be the first time Republicans control both houses of Congress for consecutive sessions in 68 years. They won both chambers in 1994 for the first time in 40 years.

In 34 races, Republicans picked up three Senate seats, in Alabama, Nebraska and Clinton's home state of Arkansas, and were leading in a closely contested race for the Oregon seat held by a retiring Republican. Democrats toppled a Republican incumbent in South Dakota.

If Republicans hold on to Oregon, the new Senate lineup will be 55-45, compared to 53-47 in the last Congress. That is still short of the 60 votes needed to cut off a filibuster by opponents seeking to talk an issue to death.
In the House, Democrats fell short of picking up 19 seats to take control but cut the Republican majority by about half.
Republican National Committee Chairman Haley Barbour said the new lineup would give his party between 227 and 229 seats in the 435-member chamber. Three races in Texas face runoffs in December.

At the end of the last Congress, the lineup was 235-197, with one independent and two vacancies. All but about 13 of the 73 Republican House freshmen who swept the party to power two years ago were re-elected, as were most senior incumbents in both parties.
Barbour said the results had ratified the 1994 vote in which voters "rejected big government liberalism" in favour of smaller government, lower taxes and welfare reform.

Republican Congressional Campaign Chairman, Representative Bill Paxon, a New York Republican, told reporters: "We cemented our historic gains and laid the foundation for a long-term Republican majority in the House."
Republicans ran strongly in the South, once a Democratic stronghold, making significant gains and losing only two seats of freshmen in North Carolina and an open seat in Louisiana.

Senior congressional Republicans said they looked forward to working with Clinton on balancing the budget and cutting taxes and the president said American voters had sent both parties a message to work together. "When we join our hands ... America always wins," he said.

Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich also sounded conciliatory, saying, "I believe that we have an obligation frankly to reach out to the newly re-elected president who after all campaigned on a balanced budget and targeted tax cuts and being against drugs and being for doing virtually all the things we said we were for."

Mississippi Republican Trent Lott, virtually certain to be re-elected to the Senate majority leader's job that he won when presidential candidate Bob Dole quit the Senate in June, said meetings on the party's agenda and strategy would be held over the next few weeks.

The new congressional lineup was expected to be a force for compromise, with neither Clinton nor the Republicans able to push through controversial legislation. Both sides have suffered political damage by overreaching -- Clinton with his failed health care reform plan and the Republicans with a budget plan that led to government shutdowns.

Despite the conciliatory statements, Clinton faces the prospect of drawn-out congressional hearings on questionable campaign contributions that came to light in the waning days of the presidential campaign.

Earlier investigations into the improper acquisition of FBI files by the White House and the firing of the White House travel office staff also are expected to resume after the new Congress convenes next January.
